title: Cooling Effect of Urban Green Space
text:
How does the urban green space regulate the temperature?

Quantifying how the structure and composition of urban green spaces moderate land surface temperature across cities. Integrates USGS 3DEP airborne LiDAR-derived canopy metrics (height, cover, vertical complexity) with land cover and satellite-derived LST to model cooling magnitude as a function of canopy structure, patch geometry, and surrounding impervious context.
Tools: R (lidR, terra, sf, lme4), Python (xarray, rasterio, scikit-learn)

text:
Aims:
Integrate field investigations, remote sensing, and modeling to reveal cross-scale mechanisms, thereby supporting the development of robust models for understanding ecosystems — particularly forests — and improving forest management to enhance human well-being.


Forest above ground biomass estimation
How to estimate forest AGB across large spatial scale?

LiDAR-based modeling of forest above-ground biomass (AGB) using USGS 3DEP and NEON airborne point clouds, integrated with GEDI spaceborne LiDAR footprints and ESA CCI Biomass products for cross-scale validation. Step 1 — Define Study Area

nyc <- list(
  lon_min = -74.02, lat_min = 40.73,
  lon_max = -73.90, lat_max = 40.82

# Approximate Central Park boundary for zone labeling
cp_bounds <- list(
  lon_min = -73.981, lon_max = -73.949,
  lat_min =  40.764, lat_max =  40.800
)

classify_zone <- function(lon, lat) {
  in_park <- lon >= cp_bounds$lon_min & lon <= cp_bounds$lon_max &
             lat >= cp_bounds$lat_min & lat <= cp_bounds$lat_max
  dplyr::case_when(
    in_park                                                         ~ "Central Park",
    lat >= 40.764 & lat <= 40.800 & lon < cp_bounds$lon_min        ~ "Upper West Side",
    lat >= 40.764 & lat <= 40.800 & lon > cp_bounds$lon_max        ~ "Upper East Side",
    lat > 40.800                                                    ~ "North Manhattan",
    lat >= 40.748 & lat < 40.764                                    ~ "Midtown",
    TRUE                                                            ~ "Lower Manhattan"
  )
}

title: Urban GEDI: Separating Vegetation from Buildings in New York City
Urban GEDI: Separating Vegetation from Buildings in New York City
text:
Results

Spatial Distribution — Footprints by Zone


Each dot is a quality-passing GEDI footprint. The green dashed box marks the Central Park boundary. Lower Manhattan and Midtown show the most mixed signal — tall buildings, low streets, and occasional small parks all within the same 0.12° × 0.09° window.




Interactive Map — Surface Classification









RH95 by Urban Zone


Central Park shows the tallest and most consistent RH95 (~20 m), entirely from tree canopy. Lower Manhattan has the highest mean RH95 (~60 m) — but this reflects skyscraper rooftops, not trees. North Manhattan and the Upper West/East Side cluster around 15–20 m, a mix of street trees and low apartment buildings.




Waveform Width (RH95 − RH25) — The Key Diagnostic
The waveform width (RH95 − RH25) captures how spread out the returned energy is vertically:

Trees: wide spread — laser penetrates through the canopy and still gets returns from the ground and understory (low RH25), while the top return comes from the canopy surface (high RH95)
Buildings: narrow spread — a flat rooftop concentrates almost all returns at one height; RH25 is nearly as high as RH95
Streets: near-zero — all returns from the ground



This single metric can act as a building/vegetation separator without any external data: footprints with waveform_width > 10 m are almost exclusively vegetation; those with waveform_width < 5 m are likely buildings or streets. A threshold of ~8 m gives a practical first-pass filter.




Full RH Profile Comparison


The RH25–RH95 profile shape differs fundamentally between surface types. For vegetation, RH25 stays low (ground/understory) while RH75 and RH95 jump sharply — a signature of a closed-canopy forest. For buildings, all four percentiles step upward uniformly, tracking the roof height. For streets, all percentiles hover near zero.




GEDI RH95 vs OSM Building Height


GEDI RH95 tracks building height but systematically underestimates — increasingly so for tall buildings. A 10 m brownstone might yield RH95 ≈ 9 m (small underestimate), but a 200 m skyscraper might yield RH95 ≈ 170 m. The underestimate arises because the ~25 m GEDI footprint inevitably overlaps a street edge at building corners, diluting the roof-level return with near-ground signal.




Quality Flag Pass Rate


Vegetation footprints pass QC at ~88 % — the GEDI waveform decomposition algorithm was designed for forest returns. Building and street footprints pass at ~44–50 %: the algorithm flags the abnormal waveform shapes (sharp single-return peaks from rooftops; very weak returns from roads) as unreliable. After quality filtering, urban datasets are dominated by vegetation and mixed-footprint shots, which partially self-corrects the building contamination problem.

text:
Step 5 — Practical Filtering Strategy for Urban GEDI
Combining everything above, a three-layer filter improves vegetation signal in urban GEDI:

nyc_veg <- nyc_joined |>
  filter(
    quality_flag == 1,          # standard GEDI QC
    degrade_flag == 0,
    waveform_width > 8,         # removes most building returns
    is.na(bldg_height) |        # not on a known building footprint
      bldg_height < 5           # (or a very small structure like a shed)
  )

After all three filters, the remaining shots in Central Park will be ~95 % true vegetation canopy. In Midtown the retained fraction drops to ~20 % of raw shots — reflecting the genuine scarcity of tall vegetation in dense commercial districts.

title: Urban GEDI: Separating Vegetation from Buildings in New York City
text:
Key Takeaways

Waveform width is a free diagnostic: RH95 − RH25 > 8–10 m strongly indicates vegetation; < 5 m indicates a flat built surface.
Quality filtering is biased toward vegetation: Buildings naturally fail QC at higher rates, so standard GEDI pipelines inadvertently self-filter some building contamination.
Underestimation scales with building height: GEDI systematically underestimates tall buildings because the footprint always samples some street-level signal at roof edges.
Urban GEDI is most reliable inside parks: Central Park footprints are clean and vegetation-dominated after standard quality filtering.
Combine GEDI with OSM or land-cover masks for fully rigorous urban analyses — especially when building heights > 20 m are common.

title: GEDI L2A Canopy Height at NEON SCBI: Comparison with NEON AOP and 3DEP LiDAR
text:
Step 4 — Download NEON AOP 2019 CHM
The NEON AOP CHM product (DP3.30015.001) provides a 1-m resolution canopy height model derived from the NEON discrete-return LiDAR point cloud using a pit-fill algorithm.

library(neonUtilities)

# Download CHM tiles covering SCBI (~4 tiles at 1 km²/tile)
byTileAOP(
  dpID    = "DP3.30015.001",   # Ecosystem structure — CHM
  site    = "SCBI",
  year    = "2019",            # Flight date: 2019-06-xx to 2019-07-xx
  easting  = scbi$utm_e,
  northing = scbi$utm_n,
  buffer  = 400,               # 400 m buffer around tower
  check.size = FALSE,
  savepath = "data/neon_chm_scbi"
)

# Load and mosaic tiles
chm_files  <- list.files("data/neon_chm_scbi", "\\.tif$",
                          recursive=TRUE, full.names=TRUE)
chm_neon   <- mosaic(sprc(lapply(chm_files, rast))) |>
  project("EPSG:4326")           # reproject to WGS84

title: GEDI L2A Canopy Height at NEON SCBI: Comparison with NEON AOP and 3DEP LiDAR
section: Step 5 — Download 3DEP LiDAR and Build CHM
text:
Step 5 — Download 3DEP LiDAR and Build CHM
3DEP point cloud tiles for Virginia are available from USGS TNM. The Shenandoah Valley area (including SCBI) was acquired under the VA Statewide 2017 project at ~2–8 pts/m².

library(httr); library(jsonlite); library(lidR)

# Query 3DEP tiles
tnm_url <- paste0(
  "https://tnmaccess.nationalmap.gov/api/v1/products?",
  "datasets=Lidar+Point+Cloud+%283DEP%29&",
  "bbox=", scbi$lon_min, ",", scbi$lat_min, ",",
           scbi$lon_max, ",", scbi$lat_max,
  "&outputFormat=JSON&max=20"
)
tiles <- fromJSON(content(GET(tnm_url), "text"))
cat("3DEP tiles available:", tiles$total,
    "| Acquisition:", unique(tiles$items$moreInfo), "\n")

dir.create("data/3dep_scbi", showWarnings=FALSE)
for (url in tiles$items$downloadURL) {
  f <- file.path("data/3dep_scbi", basename(url))
  if (!file.exists(f)) download.file(url, f, mode="wb", quiet=TRUE)
}

# Build CHM using lidR
ctg <- readLAScatalog("data/3dep_scbi/")
opt_chunk_buffer(ctg) <- 15
ctg_norm <- normalize_height(ctg, knnidw(k=8, p=2))
chm_3dep  <- rasterize_canopy(ctg_norm, res=1,
               algorithm=pitfree(c(0,2,5,10,15,20), c(0,1.5))) |>
  project("EPSG:4326")

section: Step 6 — Extract CHM at GEDI Footprint Locations
text:
Step 6 — Extract CHM at GEDI Footprint Locations
Each GEDI footprint is ~25 m in diameter. We buffer each footprint centroid by 12.5 m and extract the mean CHM within that buffer — matching the GEDI spatial averaging.

library(exactextractr)

gedi_sf  <- st_as_sf(scbi_clean, coords=c("lon","lat"), crs=4326) |>
  st_transform(32617)   # UTM Zone 17N for metric buffering
gedi_buf <- st_buffer(gedi_sf, dist=12.5)

scbi_clean$neon_chm <- exact_extract(
  chm_neon |> project("EPSG:32617"), gedi_buf, fun="mean")

scbi_clean$dep_chm  <- exact_extract(
  chm_3dep |> project("EPSG:32617"), gedi_buf, fun="mean")

# Keep only footprints with valid CHM in both sources
scbi_comp <- scbi_clean |>
  filter(!is.na(neon_chm), !is.na(dep_chm),
         neon_chm > 2, dep_chm > 2)

Results

NEON AOP CHM + GEDI Footprints — Spatial Overview


The NEON AOP 2019 CHM raster (30 m resampled for display) reveals ridge-valley forest structure: shorter oak-hickory canopy on the ridgelines (~25–30 m, yellow-green) and taller tulip-poplar valley forest (~33–40 m, orange-red). GEDI footprints overlay these same spatial patterns. Visual agreement is clear, but individual footprint RH95 values often fall below the NEON CHM at the same location.

Key findings (66 footprints, 2019–2022):

GEDI is nearly unbiased but highly scattered — mean bias is only +1.4 m vs NEON and +0.7 m vs 3DEP, indicating no systematic height direction. The low R² (0.14–0.19) reflects high shot-to-shot variability: at the ~1 km GEDI track spacing, each footprint samples a different stand condition (edge vs. interior, canopy gaps, mixed tree ages), making pixel-level agreement inherently noisy.
NEON and 3DEP agree extremely well (R² = 0.956, RMSE = 1.7 m) — both are full-coverage 1 m airborne sensors; the small −0.7 m NEON vs. 3DEP offset is within acquisition noise.
Mean heights are similar (GEDI RH95 = 17.3 m, NEON CHM = 15.9 m, 3DEP CHM = 16.6 m), confirming SCBI is a mature temperate deciduous forest with canopy heights in the expected 15–25 m range.





GEDI Bias by Canopy Height Class


With 66 quality-passing footprints across SCBI, the bias pattern by canopy height class shows no strong systematic trend — bias fluctuates around zero at all height classes. This is consistent with the near-zero mean bias above (+1.4 m and +0.7 m) and reflects the natural variability of temperate forest structure at the footprint scale rather than a systematic GEDI underestimation.




RH Percentile Profile


GEDI RH25, RH50, and RH75 are lower than the corresponding NEON and 3DEP percentiles at every quartile level. The gap is smallest at RH25 (where understory returns bring both GEDI and LiDAR values closer to ground) and largest at RH95 (where GEDI cannot resolve the true canopy top that airborne LiDAR at 1 m resolution captures).

title: GEDI L2A Canopy Height at NEON SCBI: Comparison with NEON AOP and 3DEP LiDAR
text:
Key Notes

Temporal alignment matters: NEON AOP 2019 and GEDI 2019–2022 share the same temporal window; 3DEP ~2017 introduces a ~2-yr offset that explains most of the NEON–3DEP bias.
R² at footprint scale is low (0.18–0.56): This is expected — single-footprint comparison is dominated by within-footprint spatial variability. At stand or site scale, mean values converge much better.
NEON AOP is the best reference for GEDI validation at CONUS NEON sites: same year acquisition, consistent processing, public data portal.
3DEP is useful where NEON data are not available; expect an additional ~2–4 m bias from temporal offset and different processing chains.
Waveform width (RH95 − RH25): mean 16–18 m at SCBI, consistent with a multi-layered closed-canopy deciduous forest.

title: Process-Based Models
text: Process-based models (PBMs) — also called mechanistic or simulation models — represent ecosystem behavior through explicit mathematical formulations of physical, chemical, and biological processes. Rather than fitting empirical relationships to observed data, PBMs encode our understanding of how and why ecosystems function, using differential equations and energy/mass balance constraints derived from first principles.

title: Process-Based Models
text:
Basic Mechanisms
Carbon and water cycling is typically represented through a coupled system: photosynthesis (GPP) is modeled using the Farquhar–von Caemmerer–Berry (FvCB) biochemical scheme, which relates CO₂ assimilation to rubisco kinetics, electron transport capacity, and stomatal conductance (Ball–Berry or Medlyn models). GPP minus autotrophic respiration yields net primary production (NPP); NPP minus heterotrophic decomposition yields net ecosystem exchange (NEE). Soil carbon pools are represented as first-order decay compartments with temperature and moisture scalar modifiers (e.g., CENTURY, RothC). Water balance links potential evapotranspiration (Penman–Monteith) to soil moisture dynamics and runoff generation.
Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) — such as LPJ-GUESS, CLM-FATES, ED2, ORCHIDEE, and JULES — simulate vegetation composition, carbon allocation, growth, mortality, and disturbance (fire, wind, insects) on a gridded domain, enabling climate–vegetation feedbacks at regional to global scales. Forest gap models (SORTIE, FORMIND) simulate individual tree birth, growth, competition, and death within small plots, capturing successional dynamics and size-structured competition. 3-PG (Physiological Principles Predicting Growth) is a simpler process-based model widely used in plantation forestry, driven by monthly climate inputs and parameterized from field measurements.

title: Process-Based Models
text:
Advantages

Mechanistic interpretability — processes and parameters correspond directly to measurable biological quantities (Vcmax, wood density, decomposition rates)
Extrapolation to novel conditions — mechanistic constraints prevent unrealistic predictions under climate regimes outside the training data range, unlike empirical ML models
Captures feedbacks — vegetation–climate–soil feedbacks and their transient dynamics cannot be recovered from static empirical relationships
No labeled training data required — parameters are derived from physiological measurements and field experiments rather than large labeled observational datasets
Enables scenario analysis — consistent simulation framework allows comparison of SSP126 vs. SSP585, management interventions, or disturbance regimes under controlled conditions
Links scales — sub-daily physiological processes scale up to annual ecosystem carbon budgets through explicit mass balance bookkeeping

title: Process-Based Models
text:
Disadvantages

Parameter uncertainty — many parameters (e.g., maximum carboxylation rate Vcmax, turnover times, allocation fractions) are poorly constrained globally and vary by species and climate
Structural uncertainty — different process formulations (e.g., stomatal models, mortality algorithms, fire modules) produce divergent predictions even when driven with identical inputs — a major source of inter-model spread in CMIP6
Computational cost — global DGVMs at fine resolution (0.5°–1°) require substantial computing resources; individual-based forest models become prohibitive at landscape scales
Validation challenges — process-level validation (e.g., leaf-scale photosynthesis vs. tower-scale NEE) is difficult; models may produce correct outputs for wrong reasons
Static species traits — most DGVMs use fixed plant functional type (PFT) parameterizations that do not capture intraspecific trait variability or evolutionary adaptation
Missing processes — nutrient cycling (especially phosphorus in tropics), mycorrhizal networks, insect herbivory, and hydraulic failure under drought are poorly represented in many models

title: Process-Based Models
text:
Applications in Ecosystem Research

NPP projection under climate change — CMIP6 land surface models (CLM, JSBACH, ORCHIDEE) simulate future NPP trajectories under SSP126/SSP585 for attribution of IAV amplification
Forest carbon accounting — 3-PG and ED2 simulate plantation and natural forest growth and mortality for national greenhouse gas inventories
Post-disturbance succession — gap models simulate forest recovery trajectories after fire, logging, or insect outbreak over decadal to centennial time horizons
Water balance and drought stress — coupled water–carbon models (VIC, CLM) simulate soil moisture depletion, stomatal closure, and carbon assimilation decline during compound hot–dry events
Biomass estimation benchmarking — PBM-derived biomass maps serve as independent validation targets for remote sensing-based above-ground biomass products

title: Methods
text: This page outlines the methodological framework underlying my research. Four complementary approaches — statistical modeling, machine learning, causal inference, and process-based modeling — are combined to characterize ecosystem structure and function, quantify environmental drivers, and project future ecosystem dynamics under climate change. Each method has distinct mechanisms, strengths, and limitations; their integration provides analytical robustness that no single approach can achieve alone.

title: Methods
text:
Statistical Modeling

Basic Mechanisms
Statistical modeling describes the probabilistic relationship between a response variable and one or more predictors through a mathematical framework that explicitly characterizes data-generating processes and uncertainty. Core approaches range from classical linear and generalized linear models (GLMs) to hierarchical mixed-effects models, Bayesian inference, and time-series methods.
Linear and generalized linear models assume that the response is a (possibly transformed) linear function of predictors plus random error drawn from a specified distribution (Gaussian, Poisson, binomial, gamma). Mixed-effects models extend this by partitioning variance into fixed effects (population-level relationships) and random effects (site-, species-, or plot-level deviations), making them well-suited to nested ecological data structures. Bayesian inference frames parameter estimation as updating prior beliefs with observed data via Bayes’ theorem, producing full posterior distributions rather than point estimates. Time-series methods — including autoregressive models, spectral decomposition, and change-point detection algorithms such as LandTrendr and CCDC — characterize temporal trends, seasonality, and abrupt shifts in remote sensing records.


Advantages

Interpretability — model coefficients have direct physical or ecological meaning (e.g., sensitivity of NPP to temperature)
Formal uncertainty quantification — confidence intervals and posterior distributions propagate parameter uncertainty into predictions
Well-established theory — decades of methodological literature support robust diagnostics and assumption testing
Efficient with small samples — parametric assumptions reduce the data needed relative to flexible ML approaches
Handles structured data — mixed-effects and hierarchical models naturally accommodate repeated measures, nested designs, and spatial autocorrelation



Disadvantages

Distributional assumptions — misspecified error distributions or link functions produce biased inference
Limited nonlinearity — polynomial and spline extensions help, but classical regression struggles with highly complex, high-dimensional response surfaces
Sensitivity to outliers — least-squares estimation is strongly influenced by extreme observations
Collinearity — correlated predictors inflate variance inflation factors and destabilize coefficient estimates
Stationarity assumptions — many time-series methods assume stationary relationships that may not hold under climate non-stationarity



Applications in Ecosystem Research

Quantifying climate sensitivity of net primary production (NPP) across models and scenarios
Allometric regression linking tree diameter and height to above-ground biomass
Mixed-effects models for urban cooling intensity as a function of canopy structure across cities
LandTrendr / CCDC for detecting and dating forest disturbance from Landsat time series
Bayesian hierarchical models for integrating multi-source biomass observations with uncertainty

title: Methods
text:
Machine Learning

Basic Mechanisms
Machine learning (ML) algorithms learn predictive mappings from data without being explicitly programmed with domain equations. Supervised learning algorithms are trained on labeled input–output pairs to minimize a loss function; unsupervised learning identifies structure in unlabeled data. For ecological remote sensing, the dominant approaches are ensemble tree-based methods and deep learning.
Random Forest constructs many decorrelated decision trees (via bootstrap sampling of training data and random feature subsets at each split) and averages their predictions, producing both strong predictive accuracy and built-in variable importance estimates. Gradient boosting methods (XGBoost, LightGBM) build trees sequentially, with each tree correcting residuals of the prior ensemble using gradient descent on the loss function — typically outperforming Random Forest on tabular data with enough training samples. Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) apply learned spatial filters across image grids, capturing local spatial patterns in raster remote sensing data without hand-crafted feature engineering. SHAP (SHapley Additive exPlanations) values provide post-hoc interpretability by attributing each prediction to individual feature contributions, enabling physically meaningful analysis of black-box models.


Advantages

Captures complex nonlinearity — no assumption of linearity, monotonicity, or specific functional form
Handles high-dimensional inputs — spectral bands, LiDAR metrics, topographic derivatives, and climate variables can all enter jointly
State-of-the-art predictive performance — consistently outperforms classical regression on large, heterogeneous datasets
Built-in variable importance — tree ensemble methods naturally rank predictor relevance
Scalable — tree-based methods scale to millions of training samples; GPU-accelerated deep learning scales further
Flexible output — regression, classification, object detection, and segmentation all handled by different architectures



Disadvantages

Black-box behavior — without SHAP or similar tools, decision logic is opaque and hard to interpret mechanistically
Data hungry — deep learning in particular requires large labeled datasets that are expensive to produce in remote sensing
Poor extrapolation — ML models are unreliable outside the feature space of training data; projecting to novel climate conditions is risky without domain adaptation
Overfitting — without careful spatial cross-validation, accuracy metrics are inflated by spatial autocorrelation between training and test sets
No inherent uncertainty — point predictions from most ML methods require additional frameworks (conformal prediction, Monte Carlo Dropout, quantile regression forests) for uncertainty intervals
Stationarity assumption — trained on current conditions, models may fail under non-stationary climate or disturbance regimes



Applications in Ecosystem Research

Above-ground biomass estimation from multi-source LiDAR and spectral features using stacked Random Forest / XGBoost ensembles
Land cover and forest type classification from Sentinel-2 and Landsat time-series features
Global canopy height mapping by fusing GEDI waveforms with Sentinel-2 imagery via deep learning (ETH/Meta)
Urban land surface temperature prediction from LiDAR-derived canopy structure and impervious surface metrics
Deforestation alert systems using dense Landsat / Sentinel-2 time series

title: Methods
text:
Causal Inference

Basic Mechanisms
Causal inference provides a rigorous framework for identifying the independent causal effect of one variable on another — going beyond the correlational relationships that regression and machine learning describe. The foundational distinction is between association (X and Y covary) and causation (X produces Y when manipulated), formalized through two complementary traditions: the potential outcomes framework (Rubin, Neyman) and structural causal models (Pearl).
Directed Acyclic Graphs (DAGs) represent causal structures as graphs where nodes are variables and directed edges encode assumed causal directions. DAGs identify which variables must be conditioned on (confounders) or must not be conditioned on (mediators, colliders) to estimate an unconfounded causal effect — a process called backdoor adjustment. Pearl’s do-calculus formalizes interventional distributions P(Y | do(X)), distinguishing observational conditioning from hypothetical manipulation.
Instrumental Variables (IV) identify causal effects when unmeasured confounders exist, by leveraging a third variable (the instrument) that affects the treatment but influences the outcome only through the treatment pathway. Difference-in-Differences (DiD) compares changes over time between treated and control groups, removing time-invariant confounding under a parallel-trends assumption. Propensity Score Matching reweights or matches observational units to mimic a randomized experiment. Granger Causality tests whether past values of X improve forecasts of Y beyond Y’s own history in time series. Convergent Cross Mapping (CCM) detects causal coupling in nonlinear dynamical systems using the attractor manifold structure of time-series embeddings — particularly suited to ecological systems exhibiting chaotic dynamics.


Advantages

Identifies mechanisms, not just associations — enables attribution of ecosystem responses to specific environmental drivers
Handles confounding explicitly — DAG-based analysis identifies and adjusts for confounders that bias observational regression
Applicable to observational data — no experiment needed when design choices (IV, DiD, natural experiments) are available
Quantifies counterfactual scenarios — answers “what would NPP have been without this extreme event?” — essential for climate impact attribution
Connects to policy — causal estimates of disturbance effects support management decisions (e.g., effect of fire suppression on forest carbon)
Integrates with ML — causal ML (double ML, causal forests) combines the flexibility of machine learning with the rigor of causal identification



Disadvantages

Strong untestable assumptions — causal identification requires assumptions (no unmeasured confounding, instrument validity, parallel trends) that cannot be fully verified from data
Weak instruments — IV estimates become unreliable when the instrument is weakly correlated with the treatment, inflating standard errors
Complex ecological systems — ecosystems involve bidirectional feedbacks, lagged responses, and non-stationarity that challenge standard causal frameworks
Limited to identified effects — DAG-based inference requires specifying the full causal graph, which may be uncertain or contested
Granger causality is not true causality — predictive improvement in time series does not guarantee mechanistic causation; spurious Granger relationships arise from shared drivers
Data requirements — DiD requires long pre-treatment baselines; CCM requires long time series to reconstruct attractor manifolds



Applications in Ecosystem Research

Climate–NPP attribution — isolating the causal effect of compound dry–hot events on NPP variability from confounding trends in CO₂ fertilization and land use change
Disturbance impact estimation — causal effect of bark beetle outbreaks on forest carbon stocks using IV or DiD with spatially varying infestation spread
Urban cooling attribution — separating the causal effect of canopy cover from correlated socioeconomic and land use variables on urban heat islands
Fire–vegetation feedbacks — CCM to detect bidirectional causal coupling between fire frequency and vegetation greenness in savanna systems
Remote sensing–based attribution — double ML combining satellite time series with meteorological drivers to causally attribute land surface temperature trends

title: Radar Datasets
text: Microwave radar remote sensing datasets for soil moisture, vegetation structure, and surface deformation monitoring.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
Sentinel-1 — ESA Copernicus
Sentinel-1 provides C-band Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) imagery, enabling cloud-penetrating, day-and-night observations of land and ocean surfaces.
Agency: European Space Agency (ESA) — Copernicus Programme Sensor: C-band SAR (5.405 GHz · 5.55 cm wavelength) Spatial resolution: ~5 × 20 m single-look resolution (~10 m processed GRD products) Temporal resolution: 6–12 days depending on satellite availability and latitude Common polarizations: VV+VH (most land observations) or HH+HV depending on acquisition mode and region Key applications: Forest above-ground biomass, flood mapping, soil moisture, ice monitoring, subsidence detection






Note



Sentinel-1 data are freely available through the Copernicus Data Space and Google Earth Engine.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
SMAP — Soil Moisture Active Passive (NASA)
SMAP is a NASA satellite mission designed to measure the moisture content of Earth’s soil surface globally and repeatedly. Its L-band radiometer provides one of the most widely validated global soil moisture products available from space, and is widely used in hydrology, agriculture, climate modeling, and ecosystem studies.
Agency: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) Sensor: L-band passive radiometer (1.41 GHz · 21.3 cm wavelength); active radar ceased operation in July 2015 Spatial resolution: ~36 km (radiometer) · 9 km (enhanced product) Temporal resolution: 2–3 day global revisit Launch: January 2015 Key products: - SPL3SMP — Daily global soil moisture (36 km) - SPL3SMP_E — Enhanced daily soil moisture (9 km) - SPL4SMGP — Surface and root-zone soil moisture (9 km, model-assimilated) Key applications: Drought monitoring, flood forecasting, agricultural water use, carbon flux modeling, forest moisture stress






Note



SMAP data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 — JAXA
ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 is a Japanese L-band SAR satellite operated by JAXA. L-band radar penetrates forest canopy more effectively than C-band, making it particularly valuable for above-ground biomass estimation and forest structure retrieval.
Agency: Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) Sensor: L-band SAR (1.2575 GHz · 23.8 cm wavelength) Spatial resolution: 3 m (Spotlight) · 6–10 m (Stripmap) · 60–100 m (ScanSAR), mode dependent Temporal resolution: 14-day repeat cycle Polarizations: Single-, dual-, and quad-polarization modes (HH, HV, VV, VH depending on acquisition mode) Key applications: Forest biomass estimation, forest/non-forest mapping, disaster monitoring, wetland mapping






Note



ALOS-2 PALSAR-2 global mosaic data are freely available through JAXA EORC.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
TanDEM-X — DLR
TanDEM-X is a German radar mission that produced a highly accurate global Digital Elevation Model (DEM) using X-band bistatic InSAR, flying in close formation with TerraSAR-X. The global DEM is widely used in canopy height estimation workflows and as a terrain correction layer.
Agency: German Aerospace Center (DLR) Sensor: X-band SAR (9.65 GHz · 3.1 cm wavelength), bistatic InSAR Spatial resolution: 12 m (global DEM posting) Vertical accuracy: Relative accuracy ~2 m (flat open terrain); absolute accuracy typically <10 m globally Key applications: Global DEM generation, canopy height estimation workflows, glacier monitoring, terrain analysis






Note



TanDEM-X global DEM data are available through DLR.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
NISAR — NASA / ISRO (Initial operations 2025)
NISAR (NASA-ISRO Synthetic Aperture Radar) is a joint Earth observation mission between NASA and the Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). It is the first spaceborne SAR mission combining fully operational L-band and S-band imaging radars, designed to measure ecosystem disturbances, ice-sheet dynamics, natural hazards, and sea-level change. For forest research, NISAR’s L-band radar is expected to provide global above-ground biomass and forest disturbance data at high spatial resolution and frequent revisit.
Agency: NASA (Jet Propulsion Laboratory) + ISRO Launch: March 2025; initial science operations beginning 2025 Sensors: L-band SAR (1.25 GHz · 24.0 cm wavelength, NASA) + S-band SAR (3.2 GHz · 9.4 cm wavelength, ISRO) Spatial resolution: 3–10 m depending on observation mode Temporal resolution: 12-day repeat cycle Swath width: 240 km Key applications: Forest above-ground biomass, deforestation and disturbance mapping, wetland dynamics, earthquake and landslide monitoring, glacier flow, sea-level change






Note



NISAR data will be freely available through NASA EarthData and ISRO’s NRSC portal.

title: Radar Datasets
text:
BIOMASS — ESA (Launched April 2025)
BIOMASS is ESA’s first P-band SAR satellite, specifically designed to produce the first global maps of forest above-ground biomass. P-band radar (~69 cm wavelength) penetrates deep into forest canopy and is sensitive to the woody structure of trunks and large branches — the components that store most carbon in forests. BIOMASS is a state-of-the-art mission for global carbon cycle science and is expected to directly support international carbon accounting and climate policy.
Agency: European Space Agency (ESA) — Earth Explorer Mission Launch: April 2025 Sensor: P-band SAR (435 MHz · 69 cm wavelength), fully polarimetric Spatial resolution: ~50–200 m (standard biomass products); finer native SAR image resolution available Temporal resolution: ~25-day repeat cycle; multiple observation passes used for tomographic forest structure retrieval Mission phases: - Tomographic phase (Years 1–3): 3D forest structure mapping using SAR tomography - Interferometric phase (Years 4–5): Change detection and biomass updating Key products: Global forest above-ground biomass density, forest height, forest disturbance Key applications: Forest carbon stock estimation, deforestation monitoring, carbon flux modeling, climate change assessment






Note



BIOMASS data will be freely available through ESA’s Earth Online portal.

title: Radar Datasets
section: CYGNSS — Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (NASA)
text:
CYGNSS — Cyclone Global Navigation Satellite System (NASA)
CYGNSS is a constellation of eight microsatellites that use GPS signals reflected off Earth’s surface (GNSS-R) to measure wind speed over the ocean and soil moisture over land. Unlike traditional active radar satellites, CYGNSS is a passive bistatic radar system that exploits signals of opportunity from GPS — enabling rapid, global coverage at low cost.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Launched: December 2016 Technique: GNSS-Reflectometry (GNSS-R) — passive bistatic radar using reflected GPS L1 (1.575 GHz · 19.0 cm wavelength) signals Spatial resolution: ~25 km (nominal ocean wind product) · varies for land soil moisture retrievals Temporal resolution: Median revisit ~7 hours globally; ~2-day revisit at mid-latitudes Coverage: ±35° latitude (tropical belt) Key products: - CYGNSS L2 — Ocean surface wind speed - CYGNSS L3 — Gridded wind speed and soil moisture (25 km) Key applications: Tropical cyclone intensity monitoring, soil moisture in densely vegetated tropical forests (regions where L-band retrievals are attenuated), inland flood inundation, wetland dynamics






Note



CYGNSS data are freely available through NASA EarthData (Physical Oceanography DAAC, PO.DAAC) and Google Earth Engine.

title: Radar Datasets
section: GRACE-FO — Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (NASA / GFZ)
text:
GRACE-FO — Gravity Recovery and Climate Experiment Follow-On (NASA / GFZ)
GRACE-FO (and its predecessor GRACE, 2002–2017) measures subtle changes in Earth’s gravity field caused by large-scale mass redistribution — primarily changes in water storage. By tracking how the gravity field changes month to month, GRACE-FO provides unique observations of groundwater depletion, ice sheet mass loss, ocean mass change, and total water storage anomalies that are impossible to obtain from any other remote sensing approach.
Agency: NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) / GFZ German Research Centre for Geosciences Launched: May 2018 (GRACE-FO); predecessor GRACE operated 2002–2017 Technique: Dual-satellite microwave ranging (K/Ka-band, ~26 GHz) combined with GPS and accelerometers; not an imaging radar — gravity field inversion Spatial resolution: ~300 km (spherical harmonic truncation at degree/order 60–96) Temporal resolution: Monthly global gravity field solutions; some mascon products provide 10-day updates Key products: - GRACE-FO RL06 — Monthly gravity field coefficients (CSR, JPL, GFZ) - JPL Mascon — Terrestrial Water Storage (TWS) anomalies on equal-area mascons - GSFC Mascon — High-resolution TWS solution Key applications: Groundwater depletion (aquifer monitoring), ice sheet and glacier mass balance, drought quantification, seasonal water cycle, sea level rise attribution, post-glacial rebound






Tip



GRACE/GRACE-FO is the only spaceborne tool capable of directly detecting groundwater changes at continental scale, making it uniquely valuable for drought early warning and water resource management in data-sparse regions.








Note



GRACE-FO data are freely available through NASA EarthData (PODAAC), JPL GRACE Tellus, and Google Earth Engine (NASA/GRACE/MASS_GRIDS).

title: Radar Datasets
text:
Sentinel-6 — Copernicus (ESA / EUMETSAT / NASA)
Sentinel-6 Michael Freilich is a radar altimetry mission dedicated to measuring global sea surface height with millimeter-level precision. While primarily an oceanographic mission, its altimetric data also support inland water body monitoring (lake levels, river stages) and ice sheet surface elevation change.
Agency: ESA / EUMETSAT / European Commission Copernicus Programme; in partnership with NASA and NOAA Launched: November 2020 Sensor: Poseidon-4 dual-frequency radar altimeter (Ku-band: 13.575 GHz · 2.2 cm; C-band: 5.41 GHz · 5.5 cm) Orbital altitude: 1336 km, 10-day exact repeat cycle Spatial coverage: ±66° latitude Measurement accuracy: ~2–3 cm sea surface height precision Key products: - L2 Ocean Products — Significant wave height, wind speed, sea surface height anomaly - L2 Inland Water — Lake and reservoir water levels Key applications: Global sea level rise monitoring, ocean circulation, El Niño/La Niña dynamics, lake and reservoir water level changes, ice sheet surface height trends






Note



Sentinel-6 data are freely available through the Copernicus Data Space and EUMETSAT Data Store.

LVIS — Land, Vegetation, and Ice Sensor (NASA)
LVIS is a NASA airborne full-waveform LiDAR system designed for high-sensitivity vegetation and ice surface profiling. Unlike discrete-return systems, LVIS records the complete waveform of each laser return, enabling retrieval of canopy vertical structure (plant area index, foliage profiles) and ground elevation simultaneously — similar to GEDI but from airborne campaigns with higher density.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensor: Full-waveform 1064 nm LiDAR (airborne) Footprint size: ~10–25 m diameter (varies with aircraft altitude) Along-track density: Variable; typically higher than spaceborne systems (~1–5 footprints/m along-track) Coverage: Campaign-based; missions include Amazon, Congo, boreal forests (Canada/Alaska), Greenland Ice Sheet, Antarctic Peninsula, African savannas Key products: Ground elevation, canopy top height, waveform-derived plant area density profiles, RH metrics comparable to GEDI Key applications: Forest biomass calibration/validation, tropical and boreal canopy structure, ice surface change, comparison studies with GEDI and ICESat-2






Note



LVIS data are freely available through NASA EarthData and the LVIS project website.

title: LiDAR Datasets
text:
Spaceborne LiDAR
Satellite-borne LiDAR instruments providing global coverage of surface elevation, canopy height, and biomass at footprint scales.


GEDI



GEDI (Global Ecosystem Dynamics Investigation) — NASA LiDAR instrument aboard the ISS for measuring forest structure and biomass.


GEDI is a full-waveform LiDAR instrument mounted on the International Space Station. It provides high-resolution measurements of forest vertical structure, canopy height, and above-ground biomass at global scale.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensor: Three 1064 nm full-waveform LiDAR lasers Footprint size: ~25 m diameter Along-track spacing: ~60 m · Cross-track spacing: ~600 m Coverage: ~51.6°N to 51.6°S (ISS orbital range) Key products: Canopy height (RH metrics), Plant Area Index (PAI), Above-ground biomass density (AGBD)






Note



GEDI data are freely available through NASA EarthData and Google Earth Engine.





ICESat-2 — NASA
ICESat-2 (Ice, Cloud, and land Elevation Satellite-2) uses a photon-counting LiDAR (ATLAS) to measure surface elevation globally with centimeter-level precision. While primarily designed for ice sheet and sea ice monitoring, ICESat-2 is increasingly used for global forest canopy height estimation and terrain mapping.
Agency: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Sensor: ATLAS (Advanced Topographic Laser Altimeter System) — 532 nm photon-counting LiDAR Footprint size: ~17 m diameter Along-track spacing: ~0.7 m (photon level) Beam configuration: 3 pairs of strong/weak beams (6 beams total) Temporal resolution: 91-day exact repeat cycle Coverage: Global, up to ±88° latitude Key products: - ATL03 — Global geolocated photons - ATL06 — Land ice surface height - ATL08 — Land and vegetation height (canopy top, terrain) - ATL13 — Inland water surface height Key applications: Forest canopy height, ice sheet mass balance, sea ice freeboard, lake and river water levels, terrain DEM






Note



ICESat-2 data are freely available through NASA EarthData and OpenAltimetry.

title: LiDAR Datasets
text:
Terrestrial LiDAR
Ground-based Terrestrial Laser Scanning (TLS) instruments measure three-dimensional forest or ecosystem structure at millimeter-to-centimeter resolution from fixed scan positions. TLS is the only approach that resolves individual trunk geometry, branch architecture, and leaf-level canopy structure within a plot, making it the gold standard for validating airborne and spaceborne biomass estimates.


NEON Terrestrial LiDAR Scanning (TLS)
NEON deploys a tripod-mounted terrestrial laser scanner at field sites across the United States as part of its standardized ecological observatory program. TLS scans are co-located with NEON woody plant vegetation structure plots and NEON AOP airborne collections, enabling direct multi-scale comparisons from individual stems to landscape.
Agency: National Ecological Observatory Network (NEON / Battelle) Product code: DP1.10098.001 — Terrestrial Lidar Scanning Sensor: RIEGL VZ-400 or equivalent phase-based/time-of-flight scanner Scan density: Typically >1,000 pts/m² within 30–50 m of scan position Coverage: 47 NEON terrestrial field sites across 20 eco-climatic domains (CONUS, Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico) Temporal coverage: Ongoing from ~2017; most sites have ≥3 annual scan campaigns Key variables: 3D point cloud of plot-level forest structure; co-registered multiple scan positions per plot Key applications: Individual tree volume estimation, allometric model calibration, canopy gap fraction, validation of GEDI/ICESat-2/airborne AGB estimates, 4D change detection of tree growth and mortality






Note



NEON TLS data (DP1.10098.001) are freely available through the NEON Data Portal. The neonUtilities R package and neonstore simplify bulk download and processing.





Community TLS Forest Benchmark Datasets
A growing body of research groups have deposited open TLS forest datasets on Zenodo and PANGAEA as community benchmarks for testing biomass estimation, tree segmentation, and canopy modeling methods. These range from single-site campaigns to multi-continent compilations.
Notable public deposits include:

Key applications: Allometric model validation, non-destructive biomass estimation, tree segmentation algorithm testing, leaf-on/leaf-off structure comparison, plant area index retrieval






Tip



The lidR (R) and laspy/open3d (Python) libraries are the standard tools for processing TLS point clouds. The RQSM (R) and TreeQSM (MATLAB) packages reconstruct quantitative structural models (QSM) of individual trees from TLS data, enabling non-destructive volume and biomass estimation.








Note



Search Zenodo.org with keywords “terrestrial lidar forest” or “TLS forest point cloud” to discover community benchmark deposits. PANGAEA also hosts TLS datasets from research expeditions. Australian TLS data are available via the TERN Data Portal.

title: LiDAR Datasets
text:
Data Portals
Multi-source aggregation platforms that host and serve LiDAR point clouds and DEMs from many independent campaigns through a single discovery and download interface.


OpenTopography — Multi-Source LiDAR and DEM Portal
OpenTopography is an NSF-funded data portal that provides free, open access to high-resolution LiDAR point clouds, DEMs, and derived products from dozens of airborne LiDAR campaigns and global raster elevation datasets. It serves as a one-stop discovery and processing platform for a wide variety of LiDAR archives.
Operator: San Diego Supercomputer Center (SDSC), UNAVCO, and Arizona State University (NSF-funded) Data types available: - Airborne LiDAR point clouds — NCALM, B4 Fault Zone, EarthScope campaigns, CoastalDEM collections - Global DEMs — SRTM (30 m/90 m), ALOS World 3D (30 m), CopDEM (30 m/90 m), TanDEM-X (90 m public release) - Community-contributed datasets — Research-grade campaigns from universities and agencies worldwide Spatial resolution: Ranges from ~0.25 m (high-density airborne LiDAR) to 30–90 m (global DEMs) On-demand processing: Users can request point cloud derivatives (bare-earth DEM, DSM, slope, hillshade) processed directly in the cloud without local downloads Key applications: Geomorphology, fault mapping, forest structure, urban morphology, coastal change, landslide monitoring






Note



OpenTopography datasets are freely accessible at OpenTopography.org. Many datasets also offer direct API access for programmatic download.









Note



USGS 3DEP data are available via the USGS National Map. NEON AOP data are available via the NEON Data Portal. Visualizations produced with lidR, plotly, and leaflet in R.

title: Field Investigation Datasets

FIA — Forest Inventory and Analysis
The USDA Forest Service Forest Inventory and Analysis (FIA) program is the nation’s continuous forest census. FIA plots are systematically distributed across all forested land in the United States and remeasured on a roughly 5–10 year cycle. Each plot records tree species, diameter at breast height (DBH), height, crown class, and site conditions, providing a statistically representative sample of forest composition and structure at national, regional, and state scales.
Source: USDA Forest Service FIA Program Coverage: Contiguous United States, Alaska, Hawaii, and Pacific Islands Key variables: Species, DBH, tree height, basal area, biomass estimates, forest type, ownership

NEON — National Ecological Observatory Network
The NEON Terrestrial Observation System collects standardized, long-term ecological data across 81 field sites spanning major climate and vegetation domains in the United States. Vegetation structure data include woody plant cover and height surveys, distributed plot stem maps, and individual tree measurements, designed to align directly with NEON’s airborne LiDAR collections for multi-scale validation.
Source: National Ecological Observatory Network Coverage: 81 sites across 20 eco-climatic domains in the U.S. Key variables: Woody plant percent cover, plant height, stem diameter, species identity, plant phenology






Note



NEON field data are freely available through the NEON Data Portal.

title: Field Investigation Datasets
text:
GBIF — Global Biodiversity Information Facility
GBIF is the world’s largest open-access aggregator of species occurrence records, mobilizing observation data from museums, herbaria, citizen science platforms (e.g., iNaturalist), government surveys, and research expeditions into a single freely searchable database. With over 2.5 billion georeferenced occurrence records spanning plants, animals, fungi, and microbes, it is the primary global resource for macroecological and biogeographic analysis.
Operator: GBIF Secretariat (Copenhagen, Denmark) — international intergovernmental organization Coverage: Global; ~2.5 billion occurrence records from >70,000 datasets and 1,900 institutions Key variables: Species name (with taxonomic backbone harmonization), geographic coordinates (lat/lon), date, observation type (specimen, human observation, machine observation), data quality flags Temporal range: Historical records from 1600s to present; density increases sharply from ~2000 onward with citizen science growth Key applications: Species distribution modeling (SDM), climate–biodiversity relationships, phenology trend analysis, invasive species tracking, biodiversity–ecosystem function studies






Note



GBIF data are freely available through GBIF.org with a DOI-citable download system. R users can access data programmatically via the rgbif package.

title: Field Investigation Datasets
text:
TRY — Plant Trait Database
TRY is a global database of plant functional traits, assembling standardized measurements of morphological, physiological, and biochemical plant characteristics from field campaigns and published literature worldwide. It is the primary reference database for understanding how plant strategies vary across species, biomes, and environmental gradients — essential for parameterizing global vegetation models and linking remote sensing observations to plant function.
Operated by: Max Planck Institute for Biogeochemistry (Jena, Germany); supported by the iDiv German Centre for Integrative Biodiversity Research Coverage: >280,000 plant taxa; >16 million trait measurements; global coverage across all major biomes Key traits available: Specific leaf area (SLA), leaf nitrogen and phosphorus content, wood density, plant height, leaf dry matter content, photosynthetic capacity (Vcmax), seed mass, root morphology, hydraulic traits Key applications: Global vegetation model parameterization, trait-based ecology, remote sensing of plant functional types, climate sensitivity analysis, global carbon cycle modeling






Tip



TRY is widely used to calibrate the relationships between spectral remote sensing (e.g., hyperspectral leaf traits) and measured plant functional properties — bridging remote observations to mechanistic vegetation models.








Note



TRY data are freely available (registration required) at TRY Plant Trait Database. The R package rtry supports structured data download and formatting.

title: Field Investigation Datasets
text:
CTFS-ForestGEO — Global Forest Dynamics Plots
CTFS-ForestGEO (Center for Tropical Forest Science – Forest Global Earth Observatory) is a global network of long-term forest dynamics research plots. Each plot is large (typically 25–52 ha), in which every woody stem ≥1 cm DBH is tagged, mapped, measured, and identified to species on a ~5-year resurvey cycle. The network spans tropical, subtropical, and temperate forests, providing some of the most detailed long-term records of forest demographic processes available anywhere.
Operator: Smithsonian Tropical Research Institute (STRI) in partnership with global institutions Coverage: 75+ plots across 27 countries; sites in tropical America, Africa, Asia, and temperate North America and Europe Plot size: Typically 25–52 ha per site (~1 ha to 60 ha range) Key variables: Species identity, stem diameter (DBH), spatial coordinates within plot, growth rates, mortality, recruitment, canopy position, wood density Temporal range: Many plots have >20 years of census data; some exceed 40 years Key applications: Forest carbon dynamics and turnover, tropical forest biomass, biodiversity–productivity relationships, climate sensitivity of tree growth, validation of remote sensing biomass products






Note



CTFS-ForestGEO data are available (data request required) through the ForestGEO data portal.

title: Field Investigation Datasets
text:
FLUXNET — Global Eddy Covariance Network
FLUXNET is a global network of micrometeorological measurement towers that use the eddy covariance technique to continuously monitor the exchange of carbon dioxide, water vapor, and energy between ecosystems and the atmosphere. Tower data provide continuous, multi-year records of ecosystem-scale carbon uptake (GPP), ecosystem respiration, net ecosystem exchange (NEE), and evapotranspiration — the ground truth for calibrating and validating remote sensing products of carbon flux and surface energy balance.
Operator: Distributed global network coordinated by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (LBNL); regional networks include AmeriFlux, ICOS (Europe), AsiaFlux, OzFlux, and others Coverage: >900 registered sites globally; ~400+ sites with data available in FLUXNET2015 data release Key variables: Net Ecosystem Exchange (NEE), Gross Primary Production (GPP), Ecosystem Respiration (Reco), Latent Heat (LE), Sensible Heat (H), meteorological drivers (air temperature, VPD, precipitation, radiation) Temporal resolution: Half-hourly raw data; daily, monthly, and annual aggregations available Temporal range: Many sites have 5–20+ year records; network-wide data release (FLUXNET2015) covers up to 2014; AmeriFlux and ICOS provide more recent data Key applications: Calibrating satellite GPP products (MODIS MOD17, GOSIF, TROPOMI SIF), validating GEDI and ICESat-2 biomass estimates, understanding seasonal and interannual carbon flux variability, ecosystem carbon budget closure, drought impacts on carbon uptake






Tip



FLUXNET tower GPP is the primary benchmark for validating remote sensing–derived productivity estimates. Pairing FLUXNET with co-located satellite observations (Landsat, MODIS, Sentinel-2) is a cornerstone of vegetation remote sensing research.








Note



FLUXNET data are freely available at FLUXNET.org. AmeriFlux data are accessible through AmeriFlux.lbl.gov. ICOS ecosystem data are at ICOS Carbon Portal.

title: Derived Products
text: Gridded analysis-ready products derived by fusing multiple sensor types — LiDAR, optical, radar, and model outputs — into spatially continuous, wall-to-wall datasets. These products go beyond what any single sensor can observe, combining the measurement strengths of several data streams to produce ready-to-use maps of forest structure, vegetation function, and ecosystem state. This section also includes coordinated multi-model ensemble programs (CMIP6, TRENDY) that provide standardized climate and land carbon projections for ecosystem research.

title: Derived Products
section: Global Canopy Height Map — ETH Zurich / Meta AI Research (2020)
text:
Global Canopy Height Map — ETH Zurich / Meta AI Research (2020)
The Global Canopy Height Map is a wall-to-wall 10 m resolution forest canopy height product covering the entire vegetated land surface. It was produced by fusing spaceborne GEDI full-waveform LiDAR observations with Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery using a large-scale deep learning framework trained at global scale. This dataset is one of the first openly available global canopy height products at meter-scale spatial resolution, enabling landscape-level forest structure analysis without airborne surveys.
Source: ETH Zurich (Institut für Kartographie und Geoinformation) + Meta AI Research Input sensors: GEDI L2A (spaceborne LiDAR) + Sentinel-2 MSI (optical) Year: 2020 (released 2023) Spatial resolution: 10 m Coverage: Global vegetated land surface Method: GEDI L2A canopy height used as training labels; Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery used as input features; trained via deep learning (CNN regression) at global scale Accuracy: RMSE ~2.8 m (global), variable by biome and canopy closure Key applications: Global forest biomass estimation, carbon stock mapping, global tree height benchmarking, habitat connectivity analysis, biodiversity modeling, training/validation for other canopy height models






Tip



Compared to GEDI alone (discrete footprints at ~600 m cross-track spacing), this product provides spatially continuous canopy height globally at 10 m — useful for connecting plot-scale field measurements to regional and global analyses without requiring airborne LiDAR coverage.








Note



The Global Canopy Height Map is freely available on Google Earth Engine (users/nlang/ETH_GlobalCanopyHeight_2020_10m_v1) and for direct download via ETH Research Collection.

title: Derived Products
section: Global Forest Canopy Height — NASA / GEDI + Landsat (Lang et al. 2023)
text:
Global Forest Canopy Height — NASA / GEDI + Landsat (Lang et al. 2023)
A complementary 30 m global canopy height product produced by NASA in collaboration with ETH Zurich, using GEDI L4B aggregated canopy height paired with Landsat spectral-temporal metrics. The coarser resolution makes it more compatible with Landsat-era time series analyses and global forest inventory cross-walks.
Source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center + ETH Zurich Input sensors: GEDI L4B (spaceborne LiDAR) + Landsat 8 OLI (optical) Spatial resolution: 30 m Coverage: ~51.6°N to 51.6°S (GEDI orbital coverage) Year: ~2019–2021 composite Key applications: Global biomass mapping, carbon accounting, compatibility with Landsat-era change detection products






Note



Available on Google Earth Engine (NASA/GEDI04_B_002) and NASA EarthData.

title: Derived Products
section: Hansen Global Forest Change — University of Maryland / Google
text:
Hansen Global Forest Change — University of Maryland / Google
Hansen Global Forest Change (GFC) is the most widely used global forest cover and loss product. It maps tree cover extent in the year 2000 and tracks annual tree cover loss and gain from 2001 to the present at 30 m resolution using dense Landsat time series. The product is the primary global benchmark for deforestation monitoring, carbon accounting under REDD+, and forest policy assessment.
Source: University of Maryland (Matthew Hansen et al.) + Google Input sensors: Landsat 5/7/8 TM/ETM+/OLI time series Spatial resolution: 30 m Coverage: Global (80°N to 80°S) Temporal range: 2000 baseline; annual loss layers 2001–present Key layers: - treecover2000 — Percent tree canopy cover in year 2000 - loss — Binary annual tree cover loss (1 = loss event in that year) - lossyear — Year of first detected loss (2001–present) - gain — Tree cover gain 2000–2012 (binary) - datamask — Land/water/no-data mask Key applications: Deforestation monitoring, REDD+ carbon accounting, forest fragmentation analysis, tropical forest dynamics, fire-driven forest loss, legal compliance monitoring






Note



Hansen GFC is freely available on Google Earth Engine (UMD/hansen/global_forest_change_YYYY_vX) and for direct download from the Global Forest Watch platform.

title: Derived Products
text:
MODIS Vegetation Continuous Fields (MOD44B) — NASA
MOD44B is an annual sub-pixel tree cover product derived from MODIS spectral bands and trained against high-resolution reference data. It provides proportional estimates (0–100%) of tree canopy, non-tree vegetation, and bare ground per 250 m pixel — useful for global vegetation cover fractions, ecosystem boundary delineation, and land surface model parameterization.
Source: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center Input sensors: MODIS Terra (MOD) and Aqua (MYD) Spatial resolution: 250 m Temporal resolution: Annual composites Temporal range: 2000–present Key layers: Percent tree cover · Percent non-tree vegetation · Percent bare ground · Quality assessment flags Key applications: Global land surface parameterization, forest/non-forest fraction, savanna and dryland vegetation cover, multi-decadal tree cover trends






Note



MOD44B is freely available through NASA EarthData (LP DAAC) and Google Earth Engine (MODIS/006/MOD44B).

title: Derived Products
section: NLCD — National Land Cover Database (USGS / MRLC)
text:
NLCD — National Land Cover Database (USGS / MRLC)
NLCD is the definitive land cover classification product for the United States, produced by the Multi-Resolution Land Characteristics (MRLC) Consortium — a partnership of USGS, USFS, EPA, NOAA, and NASA. Each edition maps land surface into 16–20 Anderson Level II classes using Landsat imagery, and the consistent methodology across editions makes NLCD the standard dataset for tracking long-term land cover and impervious surface change in the U.S.
Agency: USGS / MRLC Consortium (USFS, EPA, NOAA, NASA) Input sensors: Landsat TM / ETM+ / OLI multispectral imagery Spatial resolution: 30 m Coverage: Contiguous United States (CONUS), Alaska, Hawaii, Puerto Rico Temporal coverage: Editions available for 2001, 2004, 2006, 2008, 2011, 2013, 2016, 2019, 2021 Land cover classes (selected): Open water, developed (4 intensity levels), barren, deciduous/evergreen/mixed forest, shrubland, herbaceous, pasture/hay, cultivated crops, woody/emergent wetlands Key layers: - Land Cover — Discrete 30 m classification (16–20 classes) - Impervious Surface — Percent impervious cover per pixel - Tree Canopy Cover — Percent tree canopy per pixel - Change Index — Pixel-level land cover change between edition pairs Key applications: Urban growth and impervious surface trends, forest cover change, agricultural land use, wildland–urban interface mapping, habitat fragmentation, hydrological runoff modeling, national-scale biodiversity assessments






Note



NLCD data are freely available through the MRLC website and Google Earth Engine (USGS/NLCD_RELEASES).

title: Derived Products
text:
TreeMap — National Forest Structure Map (USFS)
TreeMap is a 30 m spatially explicit forest structure and composition product for the contiguous United States. Developed by the USDA Forest Service Rocky Mountain Research Station, it attributes every forested 30 m pixel with plot-level forest inventory variables imputed from FIA (Forest Inventory and Analysis) ground measurements using Random Forest-based nearest-neighbor imputation. The result is a seamless, species-resolved raster of forest stand structure at national scale.
Agency: USDA Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station Input data: FIA ground plot measurements (species, structure) + NLCD tree canopy mask + Landsat spectral-temporal metrics + topographic variables (DEM derivatives) Method: Gradient nearest-neighbor (GNN) / Random Forest imputation — each pixel is assigned the most similar FIA plot based on spectral and topographic predictors Spatial resolution: 30 m Coverage: CONUS forested land (non-forested pixels masked) Editions: TreeMap 2016 (primary public release); TreeMap 2014 also available Key variables per pixel: Tree species composition (basal area by species), stand basal area (m²/ha), trees per hectare, quadratic mean diameter (QMD), stand age, canopy cover, above-ground live biomass (dry weight Mg/ha), snag density Key applications: National-scale forest carbon accounting, fire behavior and risk modeling (feeds into LANDFIRE), habitat suitability for wildlife, timber volume estimation, cross-validation with GEDI and airborne LiDAR biomass products






Tip



TreeMap is the only publicly available product that maps species-resolved forest structure continuously at 30 m for the entire CONUS, making it particularly valuable for species-specific carbon allocation models and biodiversity–structure analyses.








Note



TreeMap 2016 data are freely available through the USFS Rocky Mountain Research Station data portal and Google Earth Engine (USFS/GTAC/LCMS/v2023-9).

title: Derived Products
section: LCMS — Landscape Change Monitoring System (USFS / Google)
text:
LCMS — Landscape Change Monitoring System (USFS / Google)
LCMS is an annual 30 m land change mapping product for the contiguous United States and Southeast Alaska, developed by the USDA Forest Service Geospatial Technology and Applications Center (GTAC) using Google Earth Engine and dense Landsat time series. LCMS applies spectral-change detection algorithms (LandTrendr, CCDC) to characterize not only land cover and land use, but also the specific type and rate of change — distinguishing slow gradual disturbances from fast abrupt events. This makes LCMS particularly powerful for detecting bark beetle outbreaks, fire severity gradients, urban encroachment, and post-disturbance forest recovery.
Agency: USDA Forest Service (GTAC) in partnership with Google Earth Engine Input sensors: Landsat 5/7/8/9 TM/ETM+/OLI time series Spatial resolution: 30 m Temporal coverage: Annual maps from 1985 to present Coverage: Contiguous United States + Southeast Alaska Key map layers: - Land Cover — 7 classes: Trees, Tall Shrubs/Shrubs, Short Shrubs/Herbaceous, Barren, Snow/Ice, Water, Developed - Land Use — 5 classes: Agriculture, Developed, Forest, Other, Water/Wetland - Change — 11 classes distinguishing: Slow Loss (stress/defoliation), Fast Loss (fire/harvest/wind), Very Fast Loss; Gain (vegetation recovery); Stable Key applications: Annual forest disturbance mapping (fire, harvest, insects/disease, drought stress), post-disturbance recovery tracking, land use intensification, fuel load and fire risk assessment, carbon flux modeling






Tip



Unlike Hansen GFC which flags any tree cover loss, LCMS explicitly classifies the speed and cause of change — “slow loss” signals drought stress or insect defoliation years before canopy mortality appears, providing early warning capability not possible with threshold-based products.








Note



LCMS data are freely available through the USFS LCMS viewer and Google Earth Engine (USFS/GTAC/LCMS/v2023-9). Annual updates are released each year.

title: Derived Products
section: ESA WorldCover — Global Land Cover at 10 m (ESA Copernicus)
text:
ESA WorldCover — Global Land Cover at 10 m (ESA Copernicus)
ESA WorldCover is a global 10 m land cover product produced by ESA under the Copernicus Global Land Service, fusing Sentinel-1 SAR and Sentinel-2 multispectral imagery to achieve global land surface classification at the highest resolution publicly available at planetary scale. Two editions have been released (2020 and 2021), each providing a 11-class annual snapshot of global land cover.
Agency: ESA Copernicus / produced by VITO, Brockmann Consult, CS, Gamma Remote Sensing, IIASA, WUR Input sensors: Sentinel-2 MSI (optical) + Sentinel-1 SAR (C-band) Spatial resolution: 10 m Coverage: Global (all land, including Antarctica) Editions: WorldCover 2020 · WorldCover 2021 Land cover classes (11): Tree cover · Shrubland · Grassland · Cropland · Built-up · Bare/sparse vegetation · Snow & ice · Permanent water bodies · Herbaceous wetland · Mangroves · Moss & lichen Overall accuracy: ~75% (global); higher in temperate regions, lower in tropical forests and mixed agricultural landscapes Key applications: Global habitat extent, deforestation frontiers, urban expansion, wetland mapping, food security monitoring, regional land use planning, validation baseline for coarser products






Note



ESA WorldCover is freely available through the ESA WorldCover portal, Copernicus Data Space, and Google Earth Engine (ESA/WorldCover/v100 for 2020, ESA/WorldCover/v200 for 2021).

title: Derived Products
section: ESA CCI Land Cover — Global Land Cover at 100 m (ESA / C3S)
text:
ESA CCI Land Cover — Global Land Cover at 100 m (ESA / C3S)
ESA CCI Land Cover (and its continuation under the Copernicus Climate Change Service, C3S) is a global annual land cover product spanning 1992 to present. The 300 m archive (1992–2015) is complemented by the Copernicus Global Land Cover (CGLS-LC100) product at 100 m, providing annual global land cover maps from 2015 to 2019 with continuous fractional cover layers alongside the discrete classification.
Agency: ESA Climate Change Initiative (CCI) / Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S) / Copernicus Global Land Service (CGLS) Input sensors: MERIS (300 m archive) · PROBA-V 100 m (CGLS-LC100 2015–2019) · Sentinel-3 (post-2020 continuation) Spatial resolution: - ESA CCI LC — 300 m (1992–2020 annual archive) - CGLS-LC100 — 100 m (2015–2019 annual) Coverage: Global Temporal coverage: Annual maps 1992–present (300 m); 2015–2019 (100 m) Classification system: 22 land cover classes (FAO LCCS-compatible) CGLS-LC100 additional layers (continuous fields): - Tree cover fraction · Grass cover fraction · Shrub cover fraction - Urban built-up fraction · Permanent water fraction · Bare cover fraction Key applications: Global long-term land cover change (30-year archive), climate model land surface parameterization, biodiversity and habitat trend analysis, carbon cycle assessments, comparison with finer-resolution products (WorldCover, NLCD)






Tip



The 300 m annual archive back to 1992 is ESA CCI LC’s unique strength — no other global product provides a comparable continuous multi-decadal land cover time series, making it indispensable for studies of long-term LULC change and its climate feedbacks.








Note



ESA CCI Land Cover (300 m) is freely available from the ESA CCI LC viewer and Google Earth Engine (ESA/CCI/FireCCI/5_1 and ESA/GLOBCOVER_L4_200901_200912_V2_3). CGLS-LC100 (100 m) is available from the Copernicus Global Land Service and GEE (COPERNICUS/Landcover/100m/Proba-V-C3/Global).

title: Derived Products
section: CMIP6 — Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (WCRP)
text:
CMIP6 — Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Phase 6 (WCRP)
CMIP6 is the sixth phase of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project, coordinated by the World Climate Research Programme (WCRP). It provides the most comprehensive and widely used multi-model ensemble of Earth System Model (ESM) simulations for historical climate and future projections, forming the scientific backbone of the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report (AR6). CMIP6 models simulate the fully coupled atmosphere–ocean–land–ice system and output hundreds of variables relevant to ecosystem research, including surface temperature, precipitation, solar radiation, soil moisture, and terrestrial carbon fluxes.
Coordinating body: World Climate Research Programme (WCRP) — Coupled Model Intercomparison Project Number of models: ~100 ESMs from ~50 modeling centers worldwide Simulation types: - Historical — 1850–2014, driven by observed forcings (greenhouse gases, aerosols, land use) - ScenarioMIP projections — 2015–2100 under four Shared Socioeconomic Pathways: - SSP1-2.6 (low emissions, ~+1.5–2°C by 2100) - SSP2-4.5 (intermediate emissions) - SSP3-7.0 (high emissions) - SSP5-8.5 (very high emissions, ~+4–5°C by 2100) Key ecosystem-relevant variables: - tas — Near-surface air temperature (2 m) - pr — Precipitation - npp — Net Primary Production - gpp — Gross Primary Production - mrso — Soil moisture - hurs — Near-surface relative humidity - rsds — Surface downwelling shortwave radiation Spatial resolution: Typically 1°–2° (atmosphere); some high-resolution models at 0.25°–0.5° Temporal resolution: Monthly outputs (standard); daily available for select variables and models






Tip



For ecosystem IAV studies, CMIP6 daily or monthly tas, pr, and npp outputs under SSP126 and SSP585 form the standard multi-model ensemble used to characterize future climate–NPP relationships and extreme event attribution — as employed in Chu et al. (2026, Environmental Research Letters, DOI: 10.1088/1748-9326/ae6dd4).








Note



CMIP6 data are freely available through the Earth System Grid Federation (ESGF) node network. Select variables are also accessible via Google Earth Engine and Copernicus Climate Data Store (CDS).

title: Derived Products
section: TRENDY — Trends in Net Land–Atmosphere Carbon Exchange (Multi-Model DGVM Ensemble)
text:
TRENDY — Trends in Net Land–Atmosphere Carbon Exchange (Multi-Model DGVM Ensemble)
TRENDY is a coordinated multi-model benchmarking initiative that runs an ensemble of state-of-the-art Dynamic Global Vegetation Models (DGVMs) under identical forcing conditions, producing standardized outputs of terrestrial carbon, water, and energy fluxes. TRENDY results underpin the annual Global Carbon Budget published by the Global Carbon Project, providing the model-based estimate of the global land carbon sink and its interannual variability.
Coordinating body: Global Carbon Project / University of Exeter (led by Stephen Sitch and Pierre Friedlingstein) Participating models (selected): ORCHIDEE · LPJ-GUESS · CLM5 · CABLE-POP · JULES · VISIT · SDGVM · ISAM · YIBs · CLASSIC · DLEM · OCN · JSBACH Number of models: ~18 DGVMs (varies by annual version) Simulation protocols: | Simulation | CO₂ | Climate | Land Use | |—|—|—|—| | S0 | Pre-industrial fixed | Pre-industrial fixed | Pre-industrial fixed (control) | | S1 | Transient | Pre-industrial fixed | Pre-industrial fixed | | S2 | Transient | Transient (observed) | Pre-industrial fixed | | S3 | Transient | Transient (observed) | Transient (observed) |
Comparing S2 vs. S1 isolates the climate effect; S3 vs. S2 isolates the land use effect; S3 vs. S0 gives the total change.
Climate forcing: CRU-JRA (bias-corrected ERA-reanalysis + CRU observations), updated annually Key output variables: GPP · NPP · NEE · Rh (heterotrophic respiration) · Vegetation carbon · Soil carbon · Evapotranspiration · Runoff Spatial resolution: 0.5° × 0.5° global grid Temporal resolution: Monthly; some models provide daily Temporal coverage: 1700 or 1850 to present (updated annually with each Global Carbon Budget release)






Tip



TRENDY’s S2 simulation protocol — transient CO₂ and observed climate, fixed land use — is the standard reference for isolating the climate-driven component of terrestrial NPP variability, making it directly comparable to observation-based remote sensing products (MODIS MOD17, GLASS NPP) and CMIP6 model projections for attribution studies.








Note



TRENDY model outputs are available upon request to the TRENDY coordinators via the TRENDY project page. Annual Global Carbon Budget data (which include TRENDY ensemble summaries) are freely published at Global Carbon Project and archived on ICOS Carbon Portal.

title: Datasets — Introduction
text: Modern ecological and environmental research requires observations spanning multiple platforms, spatial resolutions, and temporal depths. No single sensor or dataset provides a complete picture of ecosystem structure, function, and change — the strength of contemporary analysis lies in integrating complementary data streams that together constrain what no individual source can resolve alone.

title: Datasets — Introduction
text:
Why Multi-Source Data Integration?
Ecosystems operate across a vast range of scales: individual tree crowns at sub-meter resolution, forest stands at tens of meters, landscapes at kilometers, and biomes at continental to global extents. Similarly, ecological processes unfold across timescales from diurnal photosynthetic cycles to century-long successional dynamics. A single sensor designed for one scale inevitably sacrifices information at others.
Multi-source data integration addresses this by combining:

High spatial resolution measurements (airborne LiDAR, NAIP) for fine-scale structural detail
High temporal frequency observations (MODIS, GOES, VIIRS) for phenological and disturbance dynamics
Long historical archives (Landsat since 1972, FIA since the 1930s) for decadal trend detection
Global coverage (GEDI, ICESat-2, Sentinel missions) for analyses beyond locally surveyed regions
Ground truth (field inventory plots, eddy covariance towers) for model calibration and validation

When combined, these sources enable analyses that are simultaneously spatially explicit, temporally consistent, and ecologically interpretable.

title: Datasets — Introduction
text:
Cross-Scale Validation Framework
A core principle underlying the use of these datasets is cross-scale validation: measurements from one platform are used to evaluate or calibrate estimates from another. Common validation chains include:

Field plots → Airborne LiDAR → Spaceborne LiDAR (GEDI) → Global maps for above-ground biomass
Eddy covariance towers (FLUXNET) → MODIS/Sentinel-2 → Global GPP products for carbon flux
Airborne LiDAR (NEON AOP) → ICESat-2/GEDI footprints → Global canopy height for forest structure

Each transition up the scale ladder introduces assumptions and uncertainties; a transparent multi-source framework makes those assumptions explicit and testable.
